title: Supreme Court 'recalibrates' damages for criminal raps

Trigger warning: Mentions of rape, abuse

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court (SC) has increased the amounts of civil damages awarded to victims in criminal cases, introducing a recalibrated compensation framework designed to ensure consistency and reflect the gravity of criminal offenses.

In a statement on Tuesday, November 17, the Supreme Court said that civil damages are not merely incidental relief in criminal cases, but essential expressions of the law's recognition of victims' suffering and society's condemnation of criminal acts.

"They are essential expressions of the law's recognition of the harm suffered by victims and society's condemnation of criminal conduct. Through the updated guidelines, the Court seeks to ensure that monetary awards remain consistent, proportionate to the gravity of the offense, and responsive to the realities of victims," the Supreme Court's statement said.
The recalibration is based on a decision in the case of People of the Philippines vs Flores, penned by Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh.

In this case, the high tribunal ordered that all future awards for civil indemnity ex delicto, moral damages, exemplary damages, and temperate damages in criminal proceedings must conform to the updated amounts set in its decision.

Under the revised guidelines, the high court established specific amounts for temperate damages to address financial losses that were incurred by victims or their families but cannot be proven with exact documentary evidence.
The Supreme Court explained that these standardized figures account for ordinary and necessary expenses stemming from death or injury while providing a consistent basis for compensation.

"The court explained that these amounts recognize the ordinary and necessary expenses to account for the actual economic burden arising from death or injury, while providing a consistent basis for compensation, when exact expenditures cannot be established through documentary evidence," the Supreme Court's statement read.
The Court also adjusted the awards for crimes resulting in death, noting that the loss of life warrants the highest compensation ranges because it is permanent and irreversible.

In setting the benchmarks, the High Court calibrated higher amounts for intentional killings compared to deaths resulting from negligence — a distinction reflecting the greater legal gravity and culpability of intentional criminal acts, rather than placing a different value on human life.
The case

Applying the updated framework to the Supreme Court case of People of the Philippines vs Flores, the High Court raised the civil awards granted to a child victim who was only six years old when the crimes were committed.
For cases of qualified rape of a minor, the Supreme Court increased civil indemnity ex delicto, moral damages, and exemplary damages from P100,000 to P325,000 each.
For acts of lasciviousness cases, the corresponding awards were raised from P50,000 to P175,000 each.
The monetary awards will earn a legal interest of six percent per annum from the finality of the decision until fully paid.

Additionally, the high court mandated that trial courts direct the Department of Social Welfare and Development to refer the child victim, with her guardian's consent, to an appropriate rape crisis center for support and assistance.
